text:

- all real work lives on **`backend`** → `af64ee0`

So every isolated agent was being cut from a months-stale docs commit. Let me fix the setting properly.

The settings watcher may not pick up a file that didn't exist at session start, so let me verify empirically rather than assume.

Root cause found and fixed.

**What was happening:** worktrees default to `worktree.baseRef: "fresh"`, which branches from `origin/<default-branch>`. Here that's `origin/main` → **`ffddded`**, a docs-only commit with no `packages/` directory at all. Meanwhile every line of engine work lives on `backend` (`af64ee0`). So every isolated agent was being cut from a tree containing none of the code it was asked to modify. Three in a row hit it; all three noticed and reset themselves, but that's luck plus the check I started including in the prompts, not a fix.

**The fix:** `.claude/settings.json` now sets `worktree.baseRef: "head"`, so worktrees branch from the current local HEAD — the `backend` branch — and inherit unpushed commits and feature-branch state.

Two caveats worth stating:

- `.claude/` is gitignored in this repo, so this setting is local, not shared. If you ever want it to travel with the repo you'd need to unignore that path or commit the file explicitly with `git add -f`. I didn't do that unasked, since your `.gitignore` deliberately excludes the whole directory.
- The settings watcher only monitors directories that had a settings file when the session began, and this one didn't exist. So it may not take effect until you open `/hooks` once (which reloads config) or restart. I've launched a throwaway agent to check whether it's already live — I'll confirm either way rather than assume.

The underlying oddity is that `main` is ~150 commits behind `backend` and holds only docs. That's yours to decide on — worth knowing that anything else defaulting to `origin/main` (CI, fresh clones, `--worktree`) will see the same stale tree.

The damage-reduction slice is still running in the main tree.

detail: Munkidori ex verified + landed (3527 tests); analyzing Prize clamp design
text:
No stray files — that `mutate.ts` diagnostic was a transient the agent cleaned up. Holding the merge until the main-tree slice releases `testFixtures.ts` and `registry.ts`.

**A correction to what I told you when I launched this.** I listed Lucario `sv01-114` as one of the KO-condition neighbours. It isn't one, and neither is any list since D158 — I passed the error along. Its printed text is *"If any of your {F} Pokémon were Knocked Out by damage from an attack **during your opponent's last turn**…"*: retrospective, board-wide, type-filtered, and carrying **no "from your opponent's Pokémon" clause**. Different condition entirely. The repo already had this right — `conditionClause.test.ts` has held the correct account since D115 — and the *newer* census table was the wrong one, which is a good reminder that recency isn't authority here.

Two more inherited claims were off: Munkidori ex is an **Ability** (on `abilities_json`), where D158's table renders it in the column Lucario's *attack* sits in; and `FIXTURE_POOL` is **290**, not the 278 that header has claimed for two slices.

**Landed:** Munkidori ex `sv06.5-037`/`-083`/`-091` — *"…take 1 fewer Prize card"* — verified byte-identical across all three printings by `count(distinct …)` over 11 columns rather than by eye. Tests **3499 → 3527**, check green.

The finding worth keeping is about D158's own design:

> **Placement discharges a condition only for a consequent that can live at the placement.**

D158 satisfied *"by an attack"* purely by *where* it put its line — inside `finishAttack`, which only one path reaches. But a Prize is planned in `planPrizes`, **inside** `collectKnockOuts`, which **all three** paths reach. So the identical printed clause costs a threaded `attackerSeat` here. The possessive isn't free either: `finishAttack` passes both seats, so `attackerSeat === ref.seat` is load-bearing rather than decorative.

And one genuinely subtle mutation result: the Prize clamp **needed two constructed values to test**. A 1-Prize fixture alone never reaches it, because `1 − 1 = 0` whether or not the clamp exists — so the guard survived being "fixed" once before a second witness exposed it. That's the failure mode where a test looks like it covers a branch and provably doesn't.

**Exp. Share is deferred with a price**, and with a specific cheap check nobody has run: it needs a `"you may"` choice parking mid-sweep, which dominates its cost — but `FIX_ONKO`/`settleProgram`'s `resumeTail` may already cover that park, which would collapse it to near zero. The seam may differ though (`fix-onko` queues *after* prizes; this must act *before* `knockOut`).

Waiting on the self-scaling reduction slice, then I'll merge both.

The sign didn't — `per` can't go negative, because `DAMAGE_DEALT.scaled` is direction-committed at *both* consumers: it's only emitted when the total is positive, so a negative silently vanishes from the row, and it renders as `· scaled +${n}`, so anything surviving that prints `"+-40"`. It also found the sentence had been sitting in `FIXTURE_POOL` **unread since engine 0.94.0** — D133's board-heal fixture had kept Skeledirge's whole attack list, so four of five printings needed no fixture at all. That's D147's failure mode inverted: not a fixture missing a printed field, but one carrying a field nobody read. And "3 sentences" was actually 2, copied across three doc sites through nine slices.

But a Prize is planned inside `collectKnockOuts`, which all three paths reach, so the identical printed clause costs a threaded seat here. Stated generally: **placement discharges a condition only for a consequent that can live at the placement.**

detail: collision fix dispatched (D157); awaiting test + sweep review
text:
The review returned **one finding**, and it's a real correctness bug in D157 — the slice I merged. Verifying before fixing, per this repo's standing rule.

Confirmed — the bug is real, and I can show the collision arithmetically:

- **Self-side** (`preventAttackUse`, line 2088): `turn = state.turn + 2` → A installs on turn 3, locks turn **5**
- **Opponent-side** (`lockDefenderAttack`, line 2311): `turn = state.turn + 1` → B installs on turn 4, locks turn **5**
- Both short-circuit only when turn **and** index match; otherwise a bare overwrite
- The gate at `attack.ts:332` refuses a **single** index (`lockedAttackIndex(...) === index`)

So B's lock on index 0 discards A's live lock on index 1, and A's Skarmory legally uses "Slashing Steel" on the exact turn its own printed drawback bars it — with the button rendered as playable.

This is D157's reasoning failing precisely where I said it was clever: it argued the field was safe to share because `lockedAttackIndex` is its only *reader*, and never asked how many *writers* it has. `types.ts`'s own doc block refuses a different merge on exactly this ground — "REACHABLE TOGETHER … one record could hold only the later write."

Dispatching the fix.

The review earned its keep. **One finding across eleven decisions, and it's a genuine rules bug** — not a style note.

**A player can use an attack their own card barred.** D157 reused D154's `lockedAttack` record and justified it by observing that `lockedAttackIndex` is the field's only *reader*. That was true and beside the point: the field now has two *writers* stamping different indices into the same turn window, and neither merges. The later write silently discards the live one, and the gate — which refuses a single index — then waves the barred attack through with the button rendered as playable.

What makes it sting is that **the repo had already written down the argument that condemns it.** `types.ts`'s `LockedAttack` block refuses a different merge on exactly this ground: *"they are REACHABLE TOGETHER and mean different things … one record could hold only the later write."* D157 reintroduced that collision *inside* the shared record while only examining the read side.

I've dispatched the fix with three constraints:

- **Prove it first.** A failing test driving the collision board before any production line changes. D153 — the last review-fix — found the review's account was *understated*, so I've also asked for a sweep of every writer and reader, and specifically whether D155's `boostedAttack` carries the same two-writer exposure.
- **Derive the shape, don't take mine.** This may finally settle the union question the codebase has deferred five times. D152 retired the "count the fields" trigger and replaced it with a shape trigger — *a member the read site must dispatch on* — and D154/D157 both answered "no" because nothing enumerated. If two locks can be live at once, the gate must ask *"is index i among the locked set"* and both projections must mark every locked index. That's the enumerating caller D157 itself named as the thing that would earn it.
- **No assumed bounds.** A second field is cheaper but only pushes the collision out to a third writer. If it takes that route it has to *prove* the bound, not assert it.

Likely a `MATCH_RECORD_VERSION` bump to 11, which would be the first movement since D155 after nine consecutive controls.

Two things the review checked and deliberately declined to report I've had recorded in the resume point, so a future session doesn't rediscover them as novel: `lockDefenderAttack` not re-verifying card identity (unreachable — nothing promotes or evolves the defender mid-attack-tail), and a redundant `disabledAbilityUids` rebuild inside `seatDamageReduction`'s inner loop (measurable only at implausible board sizes).
